title: Godot’s new anti-AI policies are their problems, not ours
author: ramaloes

comments.body: its only interessting fore people trying to submit to godot sourcode itself, right? not someone using an ai agent  to make a game with it?

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body: Correct.

comments.author: imnotabot303

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
They're worried about PR spam, not AI code itself. Open source maintaining is kind of a nightmare right now because of drive-by slop PRs and vulnerability risks. 

What they're doing is the wrong solution, but the concern is real.

replies.author: whimsicaljess
replies.body:
if only there were some sort of technology that could be used to filter out slop PRs. if only this technology was further made by companies that sponsored prominent OSS projects. 

ah well, if anyone ever invents something like that one day i'm sure they'll appreciate it and not... ban it.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
It isn't, and I'm frankly flabbergasted you're being downvoted in an AI sub. 

There's a good reason to prevent slop PRs in a codebase, but no AI at all is going to slow the project down drastically. This experiment won't go well and they'll double back by 2027 as they start falling behind and internal dev pressure mounts.

replies.author: whimsicaljess
replies.body: yeah this is my opinion as well. i am all for not allowing slop PRs but a blanket AI ban seems insane in 2026

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: It’s very very clear that they could literally use AI to triage and prune their 5,000 PRs.  Just clear out all the slop, rank the remaining in order of quality / need / urgency and then have the human maintainers look at what’s left. It would be a huge benefit to the project.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
If you're a competent programmer I'm sure they would love for you to devote your time to going through the thousands of AI codebase submissions they get to determine what is good and what is slop.

It's easier for the devs to use AI themselves than to waste time looking at other peoples AI code that has likely come from someone that has little clue what they are doing.

replies.author: davesoft
replies.body:
Consider a rifle vs an uzi. If you hit the target with a rifle, YOU hit the target. If you hit the target with an uzi, it was nothing to do with you, that thing just sprays in a compass direction.

When it comes to code, and specifically 'bad' code that causes issues, the human needs to know why they did what they did. If they respond with 'lol i dunno ai did it' then why allow that human to tinker ever again? They admit to using an uzi... anyone can use an uzi.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
There's two issues the first is engine submissions.

Generally because a lot of people that use AI for vibe coding are not competent programmers, they submit code which the Godot team then needs check to make sure it's good. They were getting an overwhelming amount of AI code submissions to deal with so it's easier to just not accept any AI code.

It's a similar reason as to why subs ban AI images, people flood them with AI content and then the mods would have to spend a ton of time trying to decide what is slop and what isn't. It's just easier to ban it.

I'm sure the devs working on Godot use AI but they are not vibe coders.

The second issue is that Godot has a similar construction to Blender with being modular where the main program is kept as light as possible and then expanded upon with add-ons. There's nothing stopping people making AI add-ons to add AI to Godot and people have already done it.

replies.author: whimsicaljess
replies.body:
for the first: that's valid reason to have a high bar for PRs (and ai is excellent at reviewing PRs to ascertain whether they meet that high bar). if they do meet that high bar it doesn't matter what tool was used to create the PR; banning AI is like banning Neovim. "we don't allow code submissions from neovim users" sounds insane on its face but somehow change it to an ai coding tool and lots of people call it reasonable. 

subs ban ai art because they *philosophically or morally oppose ai.* it has nothing to do with "too many submissions" generally, even if they claim this is the reason. the godot team clearly has the same stance but is unwilling to actually just say so. 

for the second: totally different topic entirely.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
You want AI to review AI?

I don't know how many submissions they were getting but considering literally anyone can do it now even if you don't know a single line of code, I would imagine it was a lot. It's just easier for the dev team to use AI themselves rather than reviewing other people's AI code.

As for subs I think you are greatly underestimating the amount of trash content AI allows people to create. For every one good thing made with AI there's going to be hundreds that are total slop. It's not up to mods to curate AI content. They work for free as it is.

Even the Stable Diffusion sub had to start banning certain low effort content because of the spam. This tiny sub too had to crack down on posts that were basically just low effort content advertising AI services.

Humans are really good at making slop and and abusing systems and AI just made it infinitely easier. That's not including all the karma farming bots that now make AI posts everywhere.

comments.author: thirteenthfox2
comments.body: I think they just don't want code that no one reviews getting added to godot releases. If everyone knew what they were submitting, i dont think this would be an issue. Lots of folks will write a bot to contribute open source projects without actually caring about them to put it on a resume. Then, the architects for the project have to waste their time reviewing the code.  AI and Anti-AI are both problems for godot. Running an open source project means sometimes you get garbage to clean up. AI made this too frequent for them to handle is all.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: I created a now widely used mcp for godot (godot-ai).  Myself and other contributors essentially wrote it 100% with agents.  But we have been very deliberate about it, tested the hell out of it, many security audits, much time spent trying to ensure it’s a strong, efficient, lean codebase.  And it’s working. We almost never get bug reports and have 10,000 MAUs, we add features quickly when they’re requested (if we like them ofc).  AI is an incredibly powerful tool for building good software — the Godot people just aren’t able to see it yet.

replies.author: thirteenthfox2
replies.body:
tbf with you I dont think they will stop a person who has been contributing to the project for years from vibe coding. They even say they will allow some use of AI in their notice. They want a person to take on the risk and responsibility of their contribution.

>But we have been very deliberate about it, tested the hell out of it, many security audits, much time spent trying to ensure it’s a strong, efficient, lean codebase.

You are not the problem. There are many people out there who will do none of these things.

I don't think its in a good spot, but I don't blame them for saying they can't keep up either.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: I agree with you many / most PR submitters will be posting slop.  But my point is the AI is an increíble tool for them to solve the exact slop PR problem they have.  It’s the best tool you could image for it.  Claude, go through all 5,000 PRs, rank them, recommend outright closure for the crap ones, give strong feedback on the weren’t ones.  Accept the good ones.  Any gray are we’ll have humans look at it.  Then that can be the “beta-ai” branch of the Godot Engine and people can test and use it for as long as the maintainers want before they merge any of it into main.  It’s just kind of a no brainer.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: And fwiw I submitted 3 high quality bug fix PRs to the engine.  Crashing bugs that took me many hours to isolate, repro, fix, test and document.  And they rejected them because I used AI to write the very small number of lines of code that fixed them (again, after many hours of my driving the analysis and solution process). So they’d rather have the crashing bugs than accept fixes if AI is involved.

replies.author: thirteenthfox2
replies.body:
I get what youre saying man. There should be more of a middle ground. I just dont blame em for not adapting quickly. MCPs are what 2 years old? Thats a lot of risk if your not comfortable with the tech. Godot is very successful I don't blame them for not leaping into AI whole hog.   
  
There is nothing stopping you from forking and allowing AI in your project like you have. That's the life of open source. You don't have to agree to build cool stuff. Its a good thing.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: I agree with everything you said.  Whole hog is never the way to go. But finding a good balance and being open to experimenting with potentially beneficial approaches. This is the open source / technology world after all so it makes sense for people and projects to evolve.

replies.author: Felfedezni
replies.body: Everyone has to start somewhere. If you discourage new blood eventually you'll run out of people to maintain the project.

replies.author: robogame_dev
replies.body:
Yeah but as with any other piece of critical infrastructure, they can start on smaller safer contained projects - there’s zero need for novices to start out by inserting their code into the upstream game engine. They can make as many games as they like, they can fork the engine and make as many engines as they like - and the root engine can stay at highest quality and reliability, until they’re actually able to contribute on that level.

Open source means you get to use it and extend it yourself. People complaining that they can’t force their changes into the origin project are totally off base.

comments.author: chrisjolly25
comments.body:
For good code, that is well understood by the contributor, that the team can verify the contributor understands: the godot team will have no way to know if it was AI written/asissted or not. 

Bad vibe code does have a certain... vibe to it, though. Overengineered, sprawling, duplicated. Because of limitations around context, bad AI code is difficult to read, reason about, and maintain.  

In practice, this will functionally become "No giant, un-reviewable PRs".  

Which would have been bad if they came from a human contributor too.  

Eventually, the industry will solve the problem of using AI to produce code in a way that is maintainable. We're not there yet though. I can understand why Godot would implement a stopgap like this, while the industry matures around these new tools.
